title: Juniper and the Verdict
premise: When the coffin of town founder Augustus Verne is exhumed for a highway survey, coroner Juniper Lockridge finds it empty—and a fresh body buried beneath it, killed within the last week. As Juniper investigates, they uncover that Verne never died thirty years ago: he faked his death to escape embezzlement charges, and a cabal of founding families has been paying for his silence ever since. When those payments stop and Verne resurfaces, someone begins silencing everyone who knew. In the end, Juniper must choose between turning the killer over to a justice system already bought by the founding families, or letting the town's own verdict stand—burying the truth alongside the last body.
about_author: Beatrix Thornbury is a former small-town archivist who spent a decade cataloguing county death records before turning to fiction. She writes mysteries about the quiet violence hidden in places that pride themselves on knowing everyone's business.

chapters.title: The Empty Box
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. The highway survey forces the exhumation of founder Augustus Verne, and Juniper watches the coffin come up light, hollow, empty—except for a second, newer coffin beneath it holding a stranger's recent corpse. The beat is cold shock: the ground Juniper has trusted all their life has been lying.

chapters.title: Every Grave by Name
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. Cataloguing the unidentified body, Juniper notices the man was buried with care—someone loved him—which makes the crime worse, not better. Sheriff Dane Colter pushes to close it as an old accident. Beat: professional unease hardening into refusal.

chapters.title: Thirty Years of Flowers
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. Interviewing the caretaker who tended Verne's memorial plot faithfully for three decades, Juniper learns fresh flowers appeared every month—for an empty grave. Someone always knew. Beat: the first crack in the town's official story.

chapters.title: The Founders' Ledger
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. Digging through county archives, Juniper finds irregular withdrawals from a trust signed by four surviving founding families, paid quarterly for thirty years. Beat: the dawning shape of a cover-up too large and too old to be innocent.

chapters.title: What the Widow Knew
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. A visit to Verne's elderly widow, Marguerite, who receives Juniper with terrifying composure and denies everything while her hands shake. She warns Juniper that some graves are empty because people are still alive. Beat: menace wrapped in hospitality.

chapters.title: A Name in the Margin
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. The dead man is identified as Elias Crane, once Verne's accountant—the man who kept the payments flowing. His daughter arrives demanding answers, giving Juniper an ally and a conscience outside the law. Beat: grief becoming purpose.

chapters.title: Alibi, 1994
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. Reconstructing the night Verne 'drowned,' Juniper finds four witnesses whose stories align too perfectly, word for word, as if rehearsed. One of them, councilman Harlan Pike, now bristles at questions. Beat: the past revealing itself as architecture, not accident.

chapters.title: The Second Body
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. A boathouse fire yields another corpse: the retired clerk who processed the trust withdrawals. Two deaths in two weeks after thirty years of silence means the clock started recently—and someone is erasing the ledger in flesh. Beat: dread accelerating.

chapters.title: Pressure from Above
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. The county board suspends Juniper pending review of the exhumation 'irregularities,' and Sheriff Colter quietly returns case files. Juniper realizes the institutions themselves are compromised. Beat: isolation; the law is no longer a refuge.

chapters.title: Working Outside
chapters.summary: Juniper and Crane's daughter Ruth's POV alternates. Working off the books, they trace the payment trail to a lake cabin deeded under a false name. Beat: cautious partnership, the thrill and guilt of operating beyond one's authority.

chapters.title: The Man at the Cabin
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. At the cabin they find evidence someone lives there seasonally—canned food, reading glasses, a newspaper clipping about the exhumation. Augustus Verne is alive, and he knew they were coming. Beat: vertigo; the dead man watching them back.

chapters.title: Marguerite Breaks
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. Confronted, Marguerite admits she has known for thirty years—that her husband chose exile over prison, and she chose the lie over poverty. But she swears she doesn't know who's killing now. Beat: pity entangled with suspicion; no clean villains yet.

chapters.title: Four Families, Four Alibis
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. Systematic interviews of the founding heirs reveal each had motive, access, and a suspiciously fresh gap in their whereabouts. Harlan Pike's son, newly returned to town, keeps appearing where he shouldn't. Beat: the suspect pool tightening into a knot.

chapters.title: Threats in the Dark
chapters.summary: Ruth's POV. Ruth is run off the road and warned to leave town; Juniper's office is ransacked, the Crane file stolen. They're close enough to be dangerous. Beat: fear made physical, and the choice to continue anyway.

chapters.title: Verne Speaks
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. Verne contacts Juniper directly—an old man unrepentant about his fraud but genuinely frightened of whoever is hunting him. He offers the full ledger in exchange for protection outside official channels. Beat: moral inversion; the criminal becomes the client.

chapters.title: The Missing Quarter
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. Studying the ledger, Juniper finds the payments stopped six months ago—not when Verne surfaced, but when Harlan Pike took over the family trust. The killings began then. Motive: not silence, but inheritance. Beat: the pattern snapping into focus.

chapters.title: Colter's Confession
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. Sheriff Colter admits his father helped stage the drowning in 1994 and that he's spent his career keeping the peace by keeping the secret—but insists he isn't the killer. He gives Juniper one piece of proof against Pike. Beat: complicity, regret, and a fragile alliance.

chapters.title: Trap at the Lake
chapters.summary: Juniper, Ruth, and Verne's POV converge. They arrange to exchange the ledger at the cabin, but Pike's son ambushes them; Verne is shot protecting the documents, and Juniper barely escapes with Ruth. Beat: the plan collapsing into violence; the cost becomes real.

chapters.title: The Town's Verdict
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. With Verne dying and the ledger half-destroyed, Juniper holds enough to arrest Pike—but knows the courts the founding families built will bury it. The town itself, learning fragments of the truth, turns its eyes toward its own kind of judgment. Beat: the central moral crisis laid bare.

chapters.title: What Justice Costs
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. Juniper weighs handing everything to the state versus letting the town—and Marguerite, and Colter—handle it their way. Ruth demands the legal route; Colter argues for the quiet one. Beat: the theme crystallized; there is no clean hand here.

chapters.title: Pike Falls
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. Juniper chooses a third path: releasing the surviving ledger pages publicly, forcing the state to act under the weight of the whole town watching. Pike's son confesses to the murders to save himself; Harlan Pike is arrested as the crowd looks on. Beat: catharsis earned through risk, not purity.

chapters.title: Refilling the Grave
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. Weeks later, Verne is buried at last in the coffin that waited thirty years for him, and Juniper speaks a few honest words over it. Some truths cost more than they give, but Juniper sleeps easier knowing the ground no longer lies. Beat: weary, hard-won peace.
